title: Integer and floating-point arithmetic
kicker: ENCT 303 · Computer Organization and Architecture · Chapter 5
subtitle: How a fixed number of bits represents negatives and fractions, and how the ALU adds, multiplies and divides them.

sections.title: Signed integers
sections.body:
A computer has no minus sign, only bits. So how does it store −5? There were several attempts, and you should know why the winner won. Sign–magnitude spends one bit on the sign (two zeros, awkward adders). 1's complement inverts all bits (still two zeros). 2's complement is universal: invert and add 1.

Why does it win? There is one zero, addition works the same for signed and unsigned numbers, and an n-bit word covers −2ⁿ⁻¹ … 2ⁿ⁻¹−1. To widen a number, copy the sign bit leftwards (sign extension). Make −5 in 8 bits: start with +5 = 00000101, invert every bit, then add 1: 11111010 + 1 = 11111011. The figure shows all three encodings side by side. The range of an 8-bit two’s-complement integer is −128 to 127.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: One more negative than positive value, because zero uses a non-negative pattern.

figures.caption: Figure 5.1.1 — encodings of −5
figures.note: −5 in 8 bits: sign-magnitude, 1's and 2's complement side by side (2's = 11111011).

keynotes: Sign–magnitude spends one bit on the sign (two zeros); 1's complement inverts all bits (still two zeros); 2's complement inverts and adds 1.
2's complement has one zero, addition works the same for signed and unsigned numbers, and an n-bit word covers −2ⁿ⁻¹ … 2ⁿ⁻¹−1.
−5 in 8 bits is 11111011, and sign extension copies the sign bit leftwards.

sections.title: Addition, subtraction and overflow
sections.body:
Here is something elegant: your ALU never needs a separate subtractor. Subtraction is addition of the two’s complement: A − B = A + (¬B) + 1, so one adder does both. The trouble starts when the true answer does not fit. Overflow occurs when the result is out of range: adding two positives gives a negative (or two negatives a positive).

Hardware detects it as “carry into the sign bit ≠ carry out of the sign bit”. The carry flag is for unsigned overflow; the overflow flag is for signed. Try 100 + 50 in 8-bit two’s complement: 01100100 + 00110010 = 10010110. Two positives gave a negative pattern (−106): signed overflow. Can adding a positive and a negative number overflow? Never, because the result always lies between the two.

worked.why: Two positives gave a negative pattern (−106): signed overflow.

questions.prompt: When can adding a positive and a negative number overflow?

choices.text: Whenever the carry flag is set.
Never — the result lies between the two operands.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Overflow needs operands of the same sign.

keynotes: Subtraction is addition of the two's complement: A − B = A + (¬B) + 1, so one adder does both.
Overflow occurs when the true result does not fit; hardware detects it as carry into the sign bit ≠ carry out of the sign bit.
The carry flag is for unsigned overflow and the overflow flag for signed; 100 + 50 in 8 bits gives 10010110, which is −106.

sections.title: Multiplication: shift-and-add and Booth
sections.body:
Schoolbook binary multiplication is easy, as you know: add a shifted copy of the multiplicand for each 1 in the multiplier. But negative numbers make it fiddly. Booth's algorithm multiplies signed numbers directly and skips runs of 1s. It inspects pairs of multiplier bits (Q₀, Q₋₁): 10 subtracts M, 01 adds M, and 00/11 do nothing; then it shifts arithmetically right.

Watch 7 × (−3) with 4 bits in the figure: the answer -21 appears as 11101011. The bit pair Q₀Q₋₁ = 10 means the start of a run of 1s, so subtract the multiplicand.

questions.prompt: In Booth’s algorithm, the bit pair Q₀Q₋₁ = 10 means…

choices.text: Subtract the multiplicand (a run of 1s begins).

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: 10 marks the start of a block of ones, handled by one subtraction instead of many additions.

problems.answer: Result -21 = 11101011 in 8 bits (two's complement of 21 is 11101011).

keynotes: Schoolbook binary multiplication adds a shifted copy of the multiplicand for each 1 in the multiplier.
Booth's algorithm multiplies signed numbers directly and skips runs of 1s: pair 10 subtracts M, 01 adds M, 00 and 11 do nothing, then shift arithmetically right.

sections.title: Division
sections.body:
Division is long division, just in binary. Restoring division mirrors it: shift the remainder left bringing down the next dividend bit, subtract the divisor, and if the result is negative restore (add back) and record a 0; otherwise record a 1. Non-restoring division avoids the restore step by adding instead of subtracting in the next cycle. Either takes one step per quotient bit.

Divide 7 (0111) by 2 (0010) with 4 bits. By repeated subtract/restore you get the quotient bits 0011 with remainder 1, which is 7 = 3 × 2 + 1. In restoring division, the divisor is added back whenever the subtraction leaves a negative result.

worked.why: Quotient bits by repeated subtract/restore: 0011 with remainder 1.

questions.prompt: In restoring division, when is the divisor added back?

choices.text: When the subtraction gave a negative remainder.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: The quotient bit is 0 and the remainder is restored.

keynotes: Restoring division shifts the remainder left, subtracts the divisor, and restores (adds back) and records 0 if the result is negative, otherwise records 1.
Non-restoring division avoids the restore step by adding instead of subtracting in the next cycle.
Dividing 7 (0111) by 2 (0010) gives quotient 0011 and remainder 1.

sections.title: Floating point: IEEE 754
sections.body:
How can 32 bits hold, as you might wonder, both the distance to the Sun and the width of an atom? With a trick borrowed from scientific notation. A floating-point number is ±1.f × 2ᵉ stored as sign | biased exponent | fraction. Single precision uses 1 + 8 + 23 bits with bias 127; double uses 1 + 11 + 52 with bias 1023. The leading 1 is implicit.

Step through 5.75 in the figure: it is 101.11₂ = 1.0111 × 2², the exponent stored is 2 + 127 = 129, and the hex word is 40B80000. A second example is −0.15625, which becomes 0xBE200000. Why is the exponent stored with a bias? So that both positive and negative exponents are stored as plain unsigned numbers, which makes comparing floats easy.

questions.prompt: Why is the exponent stored with a bias?

choices.text: To save a sign bit for the mantissa.
To make it twice as precise.
So it is always non-negative and floating-point numbers compare like integers.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: The sign has its own bit.

keynotes: A floating-point number is ±1.f × 2ᵉ stored as sign | biased exponent | fraction; single precision uses 1 + 8 + 23 bits with bias 127, double 1 + 11 + 52 with bias 1023.

sections.title: Floating-point arithmetic
sections.body:
Adding two floating-point numbers feels simple but hides a lot of work. To add: align the exponents by shifting the smaller number right, add the significands, normalise, round. To multiply: add exponents (subtract one bias), multiply significands, normalise. Division subtracts exponents.

Beware the consequences of rounding. Floating-point addition is not associative, and subtracting nearly equal numbers loses digits (cancellation). You should never test two floats for exact equality. The first step of floating-point addition is to align the exponents.

questions.prompt: The first step of floating-point addition is…

choices.text: Align the exponents by shifting the smaller operand’s significand right.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Only numbers with equal exponents can have their significands added.

keynotes: To add: align the exponents by shifting the smaller number right, add the significands, normalise, round.
To multiply: add exponents (subtract one bias), multiply significands, normalise; division subtracts exponents.
Rounding makes floating-point addition non-associative, and subtracting nearly equal numbers loses digits (cancellation).
